fr:title.text: Tier 2: SVG primitives and path morphing

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Tier 2: SVG primitives and path morphing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For the geometric side of Manim: shapes, graphs, vector fields, and "draw-on" construction effects. These live in SVG, animated by CSS plus a small JS layer.

html:ul.html:li: Shape morphing (circle to square, one curve to another): arbitrary path interpolation via flubber or GSAP MorphSVG. This is Manim's shape Transform.
Draw-on / "Write": the classic stroke-dasharray + stroke-dashoffset animation draws a stroke along a path --- pure CSS, no library.
Plots and axes: function-plot or d3 for live curves, or generate SVG at build time. Note our existing TikZ-to-SVG figure pipeline already emits SVG that could be animated rather than baked flat.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Theme changes. A \diagram{...} (or SVG-passthrough) macro plus opt-in loading of the morph library on slides that use it. Keep the JS off the critical path for text-only decks.

Addresses. "Output is not interactive" --- partially. SVG elements are real DOM nodes, so they can be hover/click targets, not pixels in a video. Full interactivity (scrubbing, reactive objects) is Tier 3.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: References
Context

fr:title.text: Manim-style mathematical animations in Forester

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Manim-style mathematical animations in Forester

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Design doc. We recently extended the theme with reveal.js slide decks (\meta{layout}{reveal}, see reveal macros). This explores how to push that into mathematical animation territory in the spirit of Manim, while staying native to Forester's declarative, browser-rendered model.

The core reframe. Manim is imperative: you script a timeline --- self.play(Transform(a, b), run_time=2). Forester is declarative: you describe content and let the compiler lay it out. The web-native model that matches Forester is keyframe / state-based: author a sequence of states and let a tweening engine interpolate. This is exactly reveal.js auto-animate's model, and the opposite of Manim's hand-timed timeline --- which sidesteps a whole class of Manim's timing tedium. You say "here is the equation before, here is after"; the morph is derived, not scripted.

html:ul.html:li: No render loop. The dev server (./server.sh, fswatch auto-rebuild) plus reveal in the browser is edit-to-see in about a second --- no manim -pql render-to-mp4 wait. Tier 3 pushes this further with timeline scrubbing.
No version hell. It is HTML/CSS/SVG plus a pinned reveal version, not manim vs manimce vs manimgl.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Frustration to tier. The four pains that motivated this map onto the tiers below:

html:ul.html:li: Slow render loop --- already largely solved; Tier 0 + Tier 3.
Imperative timing tedious --- the declarative keyframe model, Tier 0.
Equation morphing fiddly --- Tier 1.
Output not interactive --- Tier 2 and Tier 3.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Current state of the stack. reveal.js 5.1.0 + KaTeX math plugin + Shiki, each transcluded tree becoming a <section>, with \fragment/\vclick for staged reveals. auto-animate is not yet enabled and no tree assigns data-id --- that is the largest gap, addressed first in Tier 0.

Beyond parity. The tiers above reach Manim parity. A separate axis, structure-driven animation, goes past it: animating typing derivations, proof trees, commutative and string diagrams, and term reduction by driving the picture from its underlying categorical/type-theoretic structure --- including from existing Agda. That is where this stack can do what Manim cannot.

fr:title.text: Tier 0: enable auto-animate, the declarative keyframe layer

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Tier 0: enable auto-animate, the declarative keyframe layer

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cheapest tier, biggest payoff. reveal.js auto-animate is essentially Manim's Transform already shipped in our stack: when two consecutive slides both carry data-auto-animate and contain matching elements (by content, or by an explicit data-id), reveal tweens position, size, color, font-size, and opacity between them, with configurable easing and duration. We initialize Reveal without it today, and no tree uses data-id.
Addresses. "Imperative timing is tedious" and "slow render loop": you author two states, the morph is derived --- no run_time/lag_ratio scripting --- and you see it instantly in the dev server.

html:ul.html:li: In the mode="slide" template in tree.xsl, emit data-auto-animate on the <section> when a slide sets \meta{auto-animate}{true} (or make it deck-wide via a deck meta).
Pass an autoAnimate default and easing into Reveal.initialize.
Add an \anim[id]{body} macro to reveal-macros emitting a <span data-id="id"> so the same logical object can be matched across slides.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What you get immediately. Objects gliding to new positions, grow/shrink, fade-in/out, and whole-equation morphs (a ... block with a shared data-id on two slides cross-fades/scales into the next). This already covers a large fraction of "Manim-style" math slides. Sub-term morphing is the next tier.

Authoring sketch. A "step" is just a slide that re-states the scene with one thing changed; consecutive steps auto-animate. A \step helper could wrap the boilerplate, but mechanically each step remains a transcluded slide tree, consistent with the current deck model.

fr:title.text: Tier 1: sub-expression equation morphing

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Tier 1: sub-expression equation morphing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The real engineering tier --- the analog of Manim's TransformMatchingTex, where common sub-terms glide into their new positions while the rest cross-fades. This is the signature Manim move and the one Tier 0 cannot do alone.

The obstacle. auto-animate matches DOM elements, but KaTeX renders an equation as one opaque blob of spans. There is no element boundary around x^2 inside \int x^2 \, dx, so nothing for auto-animate to match and carry across slides.

Route A --- tag pieces in KaTeX. A \mathid{tag}{latex} macro that renders each tagged sub-term as its own KaTeX span with a data-id, laying them out inline. Pro: stays on the current renderer. Con: you hand-split the equation, and inter-term spacing/kerning across independently-rendered fragments is finicky.

Route B --- switch deck math to MathJax v3. MathJax exposes its internal node tree, so sub-expressions can be assigned stable IDs programmatically (e.g. via \cssId or a post-render walk). Pro: far more amenable to robust sub-term matching; one equation, real spacing. Con: swaps the deck's math renderer away from the RevealMath.KaTeX plugin and is heavier.

Recommendation. Prototype Route A for a couple of canonical morphs (e.g. a derivation step) to feel the spacing pain; if it bites, commit to Route B for the deck path only, leaving normal tree pages on KaTeX.
Addresses. "Equation morphing is fiddly" --- directly. The fiddliness in Manim is the matching API plus timing; here matching is structural (IDs) and timing is derived.

fr:title.text: Tier 3: timeline, scrubbing, and reactive updaters

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Tier 3: timeline, scrubbing, and reactive updaters

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The deep end, reached only if the keyframe model proves too coarse. Some Manim work genuinely needs continuous time: a scrubbable timeline, smooth parametric motion, or "updaters" --- objects that continuously track other objects (a dot riding a moving curve, a label following a point).
Do not rebuild this --- embed it. Two mature web tools cover the gap:

html:ul.html:li: Motion Canvas --- the closest "Manim for the web": a declarative-ish generator API with a live timeline scrubber. Even if we do not adopt the library wholesale, its scrubbable-preview UX is the answer to the "slow render loop" pain at its strongest.
Liqvid --- React library for interactive browser "videos," math-friendly, with playback control and clickable elements.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Integration shape. Embed via an iframe or a passthrough HTML block on a slide, so a single animated panel sits inside an otherwise normal Forester deck. This keeps the authoring surface declarative while delegating the one hard continuous-time panel to a specialized engine.
Addresses. "Slow render loop" (scrubbing beats re-render) and "output not interactive" (clickable, explorable artifacts) at their fullest.

fr:title.text: Beyond parity: structure-driven animation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Beyond parity: structure-driven animation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The main animation doc stops at Manim parity. This axis goes past it: animating the structured objects of category theory and type theory --- typing derivations, proof trees, commutative diagrams, string diagrams, step-by-step term reduction --- which Manim handles poorly precisely because its primitives are geometric, not structural.

The reframe. Manim's primitives are Mobjects at absolute coordinates: a commutative square is four hand-placed nodes and four hand-placed arrows, with no "square" as an object --- only its picture. Every object we care about is instead combinatorial: a tree of rules, a functor from a free category, a morphism in a monoidal category, an AST plus a rewrite. See the object zoo.

Layout is a functor. Write \mathsf {Layout} : \mathcal {S} \to \mathcal {G} from a category of structures to a category of geometric scenes. A structural morphism S \to S' is transported through \mathsf {Layout} to a geometric morph. Because the picture is generated from the structure, we can emit stable, semantically meaningful data-ids.

Payoff over Tier 1. Manim's TransformMatchingTex heuristically recovers the before/after correspondence from rendered LaTeX, and often guesses wrong. Here the correspondence is a map we already hold, \varphi : \mathsf {elts}(S) \rightharpoonup \mathsf {elts}(S'). Then reveal auto-animate just consumes it: matched ids tween, unmatched in S fade out, unmatched in S' fade in. One engine for proof trees, diagrams, and reductions.

This axis has four parts: the object zoo, how to drive it from existing Agda, the animation category (your "monad / object in a category" guesses, unified), and cubical paths as animations (where your existing equality proofs are the content).

fr:title.text: The object zoo: structures and their signature animations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The object zoo: structures and their signature animations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Each structure on the structure-driven list has a representation we mostly already have in Agda, and a signature animation that is hard or impossible to do structurally in Manim. The recurring engine reduces every case to a partial map \varphi between element-sets plus appear/disappear sets --- exactly what auto-animate consumes.

Typing derivations / proof trees. An inductive tree of rules. Animate: grow bottom-up (proof search, goal to subgoals), cut-elimination as a rewrite, and the substitution lemma as a derivation-to-derivation transform --- a proof of a metatheorem played as an animation.

Categories as arrows / commutative diagrams. A quiver plus a functor from the free category --- you have Free/Category/Quiver and QuiverPath (a morphism is a path of edges). Animate: composition arcing in, a functor action sweeping the whole diagram onto its image, naturality squares filling in, and element-chasing (a dot pushed along arrows until two paths converge).

String diagrams. A morphism in a monoidal category --- you have Categories/Monoidal/Base. Animate: planar isotopy (sliding boxes past each other, the interchange law), yanking/snake equations for adjunctions, and sub-diagram rewriting. This is the one genuinely continuous case: \varphi is a bijection and only positions move, so wires may want true path interpolation (Tier 2).

Step-by-step reduction. An AST plus a rewrite relation; your free CCC normalizer (Free/CartesianClosedCategory/Base) is exactly STLC with reduction. Animate: \beta as substitution = copy the argument subtree to each variable occurrence, with the redex highlighted inside its evaluation context (a one-hole context = a highlighted path to the hole), then the local rewrite.

The shared primitives. highlight, rewrite/replace, copy (substitution, contraction), delete (weakening, cut, yanking), paste (composition), map (functor action), and the lone continuous one, deform (isotopy). All but the last are a partial element-map plus appear/disappear.

fr:title.text: Agda integration: three pipelines from proof to animation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Agda integration: three pipelines from proof to animation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How existing Agda becomes an animation in Forester. The guiding split: Agda owns what (the structure and its transformation), TypeScript/SVG owns how it looks. The structures live in your developments already (see the object zoo); these pipelines move them to the page.

1. Build-time extraction (pragmatic v1). An Agda function \mathsf {toSpec} : \mathsf {Structure} \to \mathsf {AnimationSpec} --- a list of scenes plus the correspondence \varphi --- compiled via Agda's JS or GHC backend and run at build time to emit JSON beside the tree. A \animation{spec-id} macro references it; the theme's JS lays each scene out and lets auto-animate tween between them.

2. Client-side Agda-as-JS (the interactive frontier). Compile the development to JS, ship it, and let the reader type a term that Agda in the browser reduces, playing the animation live. Your free-CCC normalizer becomes a reduction engine on the page. This is past Manim entirely --- the output is not a video but a running evaluator. Aligns with Tier 3 interactivity.
3. Reflection. Use Cubical/Reflection and Tactics/Reflection to quote a term or derivation's AST directly into a spec, avoiding a hand-written \mathsf {toSpec} for the common cases.

What the spec is. A small declarative format: an ordered list of scenes, each a laid-out structure with ided elements, plus per-transition correspondence and timing. It is the value produced by the animation category or its free-monad presentation --- the "description of code input to an animation" made precise.

Open question. Layout itself: do we compute geometry in Agda (portable, but reimplementing tree/quiver/string-diagram layout), or emit only the combinatorial structure and lay out in TS with an existing engine (d3-hierarchy for trees, a quiver layout, a progressive-plane-graph layout for string diagrams)? Leaning TS for layout, Agda for structure and correspondence.

fr:title.text: The animation category (a monad in spans is a category)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The animation category (a monad in spans is a category)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: You wondered whether an animation should be "a monad," "an object in a category," or "a whole category." These are the same guess, and pinning it down gives the type of the spec that the Agda pipelines produce.

Animations form a category. Take an animation type indexed by its endpoints, \mathsf {Anim} : \mathsf {Scene} \to \mathsf {Scene} \to \mathsf {Type}, with \mathsf {id} : \mathsf {Anim}\, s\, s (the still/hold) and composition \mathsf {Anim}\, a\, b \to \mathsf {Anim}\, b\, c \to \mathsf {Anim}\, a\, c ("play, then play"). That is exactly a category: objects are scenes, morphisms are animations. A reduction step inhabits it directly as a generator.

It is monoidal. Add \otimes = play two animations in parallel / place two scenes side by side. Now compound animations are described by string diagrams of animations --- sequential \circ and parallel \otimes .

Why "monad" was also right. A monad in the bicategory of spans is a category: an indexed family M : \mathsf {Scene} \to \mathsf {Scene} \to \mathsf {Type} with a unit \mathsf {id} : M\, s\, s and a multiplication M\, a\, b \to M\, b\, c \to M\, a\, c is a category presented as a monad. So "the animation monad" and "the animation category" are one object, two views.

Free-monad presentation (for authoring). For writing animations by hand, take the free monad over an edit-functor with operations \mathsf {highlight}, \mathsf {rewrite}, \mathsf {wait}, \mathsf {paste}, ... This gives do-notation in Agda and an inspectable term that an interpreter folds into the keyframe spec --- precisely the "monad that generates a description input to an animation."

The indexed/typed presentation keeps endpoints honest (an animation knows its before and after); the free-monad presentation is ergonomic. They interconvert: the free monad's terms are morphisms of the category. Which to expose to authors is an API choice, not a foundational one.

fr:title.text: Cubical paths as animations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Cubical paths as animations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The deepest connection, and the one you were unsure where to start. The claim: in cubical Agda, a path between two scenes already is an animation, so you may not need to invent the animation category from scratch --- \equiv is an instance of it. This tree builds from a concrete first experiment up to a research frontier, so there is a clear place to begin.

The observation. A path p : a \equiv b carries an interval variable i : \mathbb {I}, and p\, i is "the value at time i." Path concatenation is sequencing animations; \mathsf {transp} and \mathsf {hcomp} are combinators (transport, fill, whisker). So \mathbb {I} is the timeline.

Where to begin (smallest experiment). Pick a structure type with a layout --- say a finite quiver-shaped diagram. Take one equality you can already prove between two such values (a \mathsf {CategorySolver}/ \mathsf {FunctorSolver} output is a ready supply: it proves two morphisms equal). Render it by sampling: evaluate p at i stepped from 0 to 1 in n steps and lay out each sample. If p is a continuous deformation you get a smooth morph; if it is built from discrete rewrites you get the auto-animate steps. That one end-to-end path --- prove, sample, render --- is the whole proof of concept.

Your proofs are the content. The equalities your solvers and hand-written lemmas already establish (two diagram pictures equal, an isotopy of string diagrams, a coherence cell) become animations for free under sampling. You are not authoring motion; you are visualizing proofs you already have.

Directed vs undirected. Two regimes fall out. Undirected (reversible): isotopies, equalities, coherences --- genuine cubical paths, sampled continuously. Directed (irreversible): reduction, functor action --- a morphism in a free category on a rewrite graph (your QuiverPath), rendered as a stepwise trace. Same "sample the interval" renderer, different interval.

The frontier (future work, not v1). Directed type theory (Riehl--Shulman simplicial TT; Max New's directed work) is the directed analog of cubical: a directed interval whose endpoints are asymmetric. It would unify both regimes --- the directed interval as the timeline of an irreversible reduction, its core groupoid as a reversible isotopy --- under one "sample the (directed) interval" renderer. Open questions: does a sampled directed path give well-defined \varphi correspondences at each step? How do \mathsf {hcomp} fillers render (as simultaneous multi-part morphs)? Can naturality (a funExt path) be shown literally as the squares sweeping out? Begin with the undirected sampling experiment above; treat directed TT as the horizon.

fr:title.text: References: projects to raid for Forester animation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: References: projects to raid for Forester animation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: External projects and techniques relevant to the animation design doc.

html:ul.html:li: reveal.js auto-animate --- already in our stack; read their equation auto-animate demo specifically. Drives Tier 0.
Motion Canvas --- the closest "Manim for the web"; steal the live scrubbable-preview idea even if not adopted. Tier 3.
Liqvid --- interactive browser videos, math-friendly. Tier 3.
MathJax v3 --- node-tree access for tagging equation sub-terms. Tier 1.
flubber and GSAP MorphSVG --- arbitrary SVG path interpolation. Tier 2.
Manim Community --- the reference for what we are emulating (TransformMatchingTex, updaters, plotting), even as we reject the imperative model.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Structure-driven animation (that axis) --- prior art for animating categorical/type-theoretic objects, not just geometry.

html:ul.html:li: homotopy.io --- the one to study hardest. A proof assistant for finitely-presented n-categories via string diagrams that renders a k-cell as a movie of (k-1)-diagrams: "animation = higher morphism," already shipped in the browser. Heavy overlap with the cubical-paths idea.

DisCoPy --- string diagrams as morphisms in monoidal categories, with functorial semantics, rewriting, and drawing (Python; the type-safety and web stories are where we would improve). Backs the object zoo and the animation category.
AlgebraicJulia (Catlab + AlgebraicRewriting) --- ACSets are the "diagram = functor" representation, with DPO rewriting of diagrams. The structure layer for the zoo.
PLT Redex --- reduction-relation visualization and traces; prior art for term-reduction animations.
Ott, bussproofs, and the prooftrees package (built on LaTeX forest) --- inference-rule and proof-tree typesetting.

Fran / Functional Reactive Animation (Elliott--Hudak) and reanimate --- the denotational \mathsf {Behavior} = \mathsf {Time} \to \mathsf {Scene} model, for the continuous/easing layer alongside the animation category.

Route B --- switch deck math to MathJax v3. MathJax exposes its internal node tree, so sub-expressions can be assigned stable IDs programmatically (e.g. via \cssId or a post-render walk). Pro: far more amenable to robust sub-term matching; one equation, real spacing. Con: swaps the deck's math renderer away from the RevealMath.KaTeX plugin and is heavier.

Recommendation. Prototype Route A for a couple of canonical morphs (e.g. a derivation step) to feel the spacing pain; if it bites, commit to Route B for the deck path only, leaving normal tree pages on KaTeX.
Addresses. "Equation morphing is fiddly" --- directly. The fiddliness in Manim is the matching API plus timing; here matching is structural (IDs) and timing is derived.

fr:title.text: Tier 2: SVG primitives and path morphing

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Tier 2: SVG primitives and path morphing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For the geometric side of Manim: shapes, graphs, vector fields, and "draw-on" construction effects. These live in SVG, animated by CSS plus a small JS layer.

html:ul.html:li: Shape morphing (circle to square, one curve to another): arbitrary path interpolation via flubber or GSAP MorphSVG. This is Manim's shape Transform.
Draw-on / "Write": the classic stroke-dasharray + stroke-dashoffset animation draws a stroke along a path --- pure CSS, no library.
Plots and axes: function-plot or d3 for live curves, or generate SVG at build time. Note our existing TikZ-to-SVG figure pipeline already emits SVG that could be animated rather than baked flat.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Theme changes. A \diagram{...} (or SVG-passthrough) macro plus opt-in loading of the morph library on slides that use it. Keep the JS off the critical path for text-only decks.

Addresses. "Output is not interactive" --- partially. SVG elements are real DOM nodes, so they can be hover/click targets, not pixels in a video. Full interactivity (scrubbing, reactive objects) is Tier 3.

fr:title.text: Tier 3: timeline, scrubbing, and reactive updaters

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Tier 3: timeline, scrubbing, and reactive updaters

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The deep end, reached only if the keyframe model proves too coarse. Some Manim work genuinely needs continuous time: a scrubbable timeline, smooth parametric motion, or "updaters" --- objects that continuously track other objects (a dot riding a moving curve, a label following a point).
Do not rebuild this --- embed it. Two mature web tools cover the gap:

html:ul.html:li: Motion Canvas --- the closest "Manim for the web": a declarative-ish generator API with a live timeline scrubber. Even if we do not adopt the library wholesale, its scrubbable-preview UX is the answer to the "slow render loop" pain at its strongest.
Liqvid --- React library for interactive browser "videos," math-friendly, with playback control and clickable elements.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Integration shape. Embed via an iframe or a passthrough HTML block on a slide, so a single animated panel sits inside an otherwise normal Forester deck. This keeps the authoring surface declarative while delegating the one hard continuous-time panel to a specialized engine.
Addresses. "Slow render loop" (scrubbing beats re-render) and "output not interactive" (clickable, explorable artifacts) at their fullest.

fr:title.text: Beyond parity: structure-driven animation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Beyond parity: structure-driven animation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The main animation doc stops at Manim parity. This axis goes past it: animating the structured objects of category theory and type theory --- typing derivations, proof trees, commutative diagrams, string diagrams, step-by-step term reduction --- which Manim handles poorly precisely because its primitives are geometric, not structural.

The reframe. Manim's primitives are Mobjects at absolute coordinates: a commutative square is four hand-placed nodes and four hand-placed arrows, with no "square" as an object --- only its picture. Every object we care about is instead combinatorial: a tree of rules, a functor from a free category, a morphism in a monoidal category, an AST plus a rewrite. See the object zoo.

Layout is a functor. Write \mathsf {Layout} : \mathcal {S} \to \mathcal {G} from a category of structures to a category of geometric scenes. A structural morphism S \to S' is transported through \mathsf {Layout} to a geometric morph. Because the picture is generated from the structure, we can emit stable, semantically meaningful data-ids.

Payoff over Tier 1. Manim's TransformMatchingTex heuristically recovers the before/after correspondence from rendered LaTeX, and often guesses wrong. Here the correspondence is a map we already hold, \varphi : \mathsf {elts}(S) \rightharpoonup \mathsf {elts}(S'). Then reveal auto-animate just consumes it: matched ids tween, unmatched in S fade out, unmatched in S' fade in. One engine for proof trees, diagrams, and reductions.

This axis has four parts: the object zoo, how to drive it from existing Agda, the animation category (your "monad / object in a category" guesses, unified), and cubical paths as animations (where your existing equality proofs are the content).

fr:title.text: The object zoo: structures and their signature animations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The object zoo: structures and their signature animations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Each structure on the structure-driven list has a representation we mostly already have in Agda, and a signature animation that is hard or impossible to do structurally in Manim. The recurring engine reduces every case to a partial map \varphi between element-sets plus appear/disappear sets --- exactly what auto-animate consumes.

Typing derivations / proof trees. An inductive tree of rules. Animate: grow bottom-up (proof search, goal to subgoals), cut-elimination as a rewrite, and the substitution lemma as a derivation-to-derivation transform --- a proof of a metatheorem played as an animation.

Categories as arrows / commutative diagrams. A quiver plus a functor from the free category --- you have Free/Category/Quiver and QuiverPath (a morphism is a path of edges). Animate: composition arcing in, a functor action sweeping the whole diagram onto its image, naturality squares filling in, and element-chasing (a dot pushed along arrows until two paths converge).

String diagrams. A morphism in a monoidal category --- you have Categories/Monoidal/Base. Animate: planar isotopy (sliding boxes past each other, the interchange law), yanking/snake equations for adjunctions, and sub-diagram rewriting. This is the one genuinely continuous case: \varphi is a bijection and only positions move, so wires may want true path interpolation (Tier 2).

Step-by-step reduction. An AST plus a rewrite relation; your free CCC normalizer (Free/CartesianClosedCategory/Base) is exactly STLC with reduction. Animate: \beta as substitution = copy the argument subtree to each variable occurrence, with the redex highlighted inside its evaluation context (a one-hole context = a highlighted path to the hole), then the local rewrite.

The shared primitives. highlight, rewrite/replace, copy (substitution, contraction), delete (weakening, cut, yanking), paste (composition), map (functor action), and the lone continuous one, deform (isotopy). All but the last are a partial element-map plus appear/disappear.

fr:title.text: Agda integration: three pipelines from proof to animation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Agda integration: three pipelines from proof to animation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How existing Agda becomes an animation in Forester. The guiding split: Agda owns what (the structure and its transformation), TypeScript/SVG owns how it looks. The structures live in your developments already (see the object zoo); these pipelines move them to the page.

1. Build-time extraction (pragmatic v1). An Agda function \mathsf {toSpec} : \mathsf {Structure} \to \mathsf {AnimationSpec} --- a list of scenes plus the correspondence \varphi --- compiled via Agda's JS or GHC backend and run at build time to emit JSON beside the tree. A \animation{spec-id} macro references it; the theme's JS lays each scene out and lets auto-animate tween between them.

2. Client-side Agda-as-JS (the interactive frontier). Compile the development to JS, ship it, and let the reader type a term that Agda in the browser reduces, playing the animation live. Your free-CCC normalizer becomes a reduction engine on the page. This is past Manim entirely --- the output is not a video but a running evaluator. Aligns with Tier 3 interactivity.
3. Reflection. Use Cubical/Reflection and Tactics/Reflection to quote a term or derivation's AST directly into a spec, avoiding a hand-written \mathsf {toSpec} for the common cases.

What the spec is. A small declarative format: an ordered list of scenes, each a laid-out structure with ided elements, plus per-transition correspondence and timing. It is the value produced by the animation category or its free-monad presentation --- the "description of code input to an animation" made precise.

Open question. Layout itself: do we compute geometry in Agda (portable, but reimplementing tree/quiver/string-diagram layout), or emit only the combinatorial structure and lay out in TS with an existing engine (d3-hierarchy for trees, a quiver layout, a progressive-plane-graph layout for string diagrams)? Leaning TS for layout, Agda for structure and correspondence.

fr:title.text: The animation category (a monad in spans is a category)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The animation category (a monad in spans is a category)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: You wondered whether an animation should be "a monad," "an object in a category," or "a whole category." These are the same guess, and pinning it down gives the type of the spec that the Agda pipelines produce.

Animations form a category. Take an animation type indexed by its endpoints, \mathsf {Anim} : \mathsf {Scene} \to \mathsf {Scene} \to \mathsf {Type}, with \mathsf {id} : \mathsf {Anim}\, s\, s (the still/hold) and composition \mathsf {Anim}\, a\, b \to \mathsf {Anim}\, b\, c \to \mathsf {Anim}\, a\, c ("play, then play"). That is exactly a category: objects are scenes, morphisms are animations. A reduction step inhabits it directly as a generator.

It is monoidal. Add \otimes = play two animations in parallel / place two scenes side by side. Now compound animations are described by string diagrams of animations --- sequential \circ and parallel \otimes .

Why "monad" was also right. A monad in the bicategory of spans is a category: an indexed family M : \mathsf {Scene} \to \mathsf {Scene} \to \mathsf {Type} with a unit \mathsf {id} : M\, s\, s and a multiplication M\, a\, b \to M\, b\, c \to M\, a\, c is a category presented as a monad. So "the animation monad" and "the animation category" are one object, two views.

Free-monad presentation (for authoring). For writing animations by hand, take the free monad over an edit-functor with operations \mathsf {highlight}, \mathsf {rewrite}, \mathsf {wait}, \mathsf {paste}, ... This gives do-notation in Agda and an inspectable term that an interpreter folds into the keyframe spec --- precisely the "monad that generates a description input to an animation."

The indexed/typed presentation keeps endpoints honest (an animation knows its before and after); the free-monad presentation is ergonomic. They interconvert: the free monad's terms are morphisms of the category. Which to expose to authors is an API choice, not a foundational one.

fr:title.text: Cubical paths as animations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Cubical paths as animations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The deepest connection, and the one you were unsure where to start. The claim: in cubical Agda, a path between two scenes already is an animation, so you may not need to invent the animation category from scratch --- \equiv is an instance of it. This tree builds from a concrete first experiment up to a research frontier, so there is a clear place to begin.

The observation. A path p : a \equiv b carries an interval variable i : \mathbb {I}, and p\, i is "the value at time i." Path concatenation is sequencing animations; \mathsf {transp} and \mathsf {hcomp} are combinators (transport, fill, whisker). So \mathbb {I} is the timeline.

Where to begin (smallest experiment). Pick a structure type with a layout --- say a finite quiver-shaped diagram. Take one equality you can already prove between two such values (a \mathsf {CategorySolver}/ \mathsf {FunctorSolver} output is a ready supply: it proves two morphisms equal). Render it by sampling: evaluate p at i stepped from 0 to 1 in n steps and lay out each sample. If p is a continuous deformation you get a smooth morph; if it is built from discrete rewrites you get the auto-animate steps. That one end-to-end path --- prove, sample, render --- is the whole proof of concept.

Your proofs are the content. The equalities your solvers and hand-written lemmas already establish (two diagram pictures equal, an isotopy of string diagrams, a coherence cell) become animations for free under sampling. You are not authoring motion; you are visualizing proofs you already have.

Directed vs undirected. Two regimes fall out. Undirected (reversible): isotopies, equalities, coherences --- genuine cubical paths, sampled continuously. Directed (irreversible): reduction, functor action --- a morphism in a free category on a rewrite graph (your QuiverPath), rendered as a stepwise trace. Same "sample the interval" renderer, different interval.

The frontier (future work, not v1). Directed type theory (Riehl--Shulman simplicial TT; Max New's directed work) is the directed analog of cubical: a directed interval whose endpoints are asymmetric. It would unify both regimes --- the directed interval as the timeline of an irreversible reduction, its core groupoid as a reversible isotopy --- under one "sample the (directed) interval" renderer. Open questions: does a sampled directed path give well-defined \varphi correspondences at each step? How do \mathsf {hcomp} fillers render (as simultaneous multi-part morphs)? Can naturality (a funExt path) be shown literally as the squares sweeping out? Begin with the undirected sampling experiment above; treat directed TT as the horizon.

fr:title.text: References: projects to raid for Forester animation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: References: projects to raid for Forester animation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: External projects and techniques relevant to the animation design doc.

html:ul.html:li: reveal.js auto-animate --- already in our stack; read their equation auto-animate demo specifically. Drives Tier 0.
Motion Canvas --- the closest "Manim for the web"; steal the live scrubbable-preview idea even if not adopted. Tier 3.
Liqvid --- interactive browser videos, math-friendly. Tier 3.
MathJax v3 --- node-tree access for tagging equation sub-terms. Tier 1.
flubber and GSAP MorphSVG --- arbitrary SVG path interpolation. Tier 2.
Manim Community --- the reference for what we are emulating (TransformMatchingTex, updaters, plotting), even as we reject the imperative model.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Structure-driven animation (that axis) --- prior art for animating categorical/type-theoretic objects, not just geometry.

html:ul.html:li: homotopy.io --- the one to study hardest. A proof assistant for finitely-presented n-categories via string diagrams that renders a k-cell as a movie of (k-1)-diagrams: "animation = higher morphism," already shipped in the browser. Heavy overlap with the cubical-paths idea.

DisCoPy --- string diagrams as morphisms in monoidal categories, with functorial semantics, rewriting, and drawing (Python; the type-safety and web stories are where we would improve). Backs the object zoo and the animation category.
AlgebraicJulia (Catlab + AlgebraicRewriting) --- ACSets are the "diagram = functor" representation, with DPO rewriting of diagrams. The structure layer for the zoo.
PLT Redex --- reduction-relation visualization and traces; prior art for term-reduction animations.
Ott, bussproofs, and the prooftrees package (built on LaTeX forest) --- inference-rule and proof-tree typesetting.

Fran / Functional Reactive Animation (Elliott--Hudak) and reanimate --- the denotational \mathsf {Behavior} = \mathsf {Time} \to \mathsf {Scene} model, for the continuous/easing layer alongside the animation category.
